tldr: Using just a single consumer-grade GPU and under 20 minutes of simulation training, this work demonstrates that locomotion policies can transfer reliably zero-shot to harsh real-world conditions, including a lunar-analog facility.
hero_caption: A quadruped robot trained in a simple simulated environment (top-left inset) walks stably in a real-world lunar-analog facility. It demonstrates that massive parallel simulation paired with appropriate domain randomization enables adaptation to the real world without complex modeling.
overview:
Developing control systems for space exploration robots has long been challenging, demanding immense time and cost due to harsh environments, safety requirements, and testing difficulties. While quadruped robots are promising for traversing rough terrains and steep slopes where wheeled rovers struggle, hand-engineering controllers for complex legged dynamics with frequent contacts and slips is exceptionally labor-intensive.

To address this, the authors turned to an approach combining "GPU-native massively parallel simulation using JAX" with domain randomization (DR). By executing both training and simulation entirely on the GPU, they eliminated CPU-GPU communication bottlenecks, building a framework capable of running hundreds of millions of reinforcement learning steps in just 10 to 15 minutes.

For evaluation, they used an off-the-shelf 12-DoF quadruped robot, the Unitree Go2 Edu. They tested zero-shot transfer—deploying policies trained purely in simulation directly to hardware without real-world fine-tuning—on ultra-low-friction slippery surfaces and in a lunar-analog facility with loose soil and steep slopes. As a result, policies trained in 11 to 15 minutes on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4070 Ti) walked with remarkable stability in the real world without falling.

This research compellingly demonstrates a future where, even with minimal compute resources and simple setups, modern RL frameworks can enable fast development and rapid iteration of robust robotic control systems for demanding environments like space exploration.
contributions: Demonstrated an ultra-fast training pipeline using a JAX-native simulation environment that completes 250 million steps of reinforcement learning in about 11 to 15 minutes on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4070 Ti).

Achieved successful zero-shot transfer of simulation-trained policies to real hardware on low-friction sheets and in a lunar-analog facility (loose soil and steep slopes) without fine-tuning on the robot.

Experimentally showed how domain randomization of friction and slope, along with curriculum learning, contributes to the emergence of slip-prevention and fall-avoidance behaviors in unseen real-world environments.

sections.heading: Why quadruped robots and reinforcement learning for space exploration?
sections.summary: Legged robots capable of stepping over uneven terrain and obstacles are promising platforms to complement traditional wheeled rovers in next-generation space exploration. This study benchmarks fast simulation training and real-world transfer using an off-the-shelf 12-DoF quadruped robot on continuous-control locomotion tasks.
sections.details:
In space exploration, environments feature many harsh terrains—such as boulder fields and steep cliffs—that traditional wheeled rovers cannot traverse. Legged robots have drawn major interest as mobile platforms to complement rovers, thanks to their ability to step over obstacles and adapt compliantly to uneven ground.

In this work, the authors used a commercial 12-DoF (Degree of Freedom; 3 joint motors per leg) quadruped robot, the Unitree Go2 Edu, as their common experimental platform. The robot is equipped with proprioceptive sensors measuring joint positions and velocities, optical sensors, and an onboard computer.

The locomotion task is formulated as a continuous-action reinforcement learning problem based on a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where the agent selects actions from observed states to maximize long-term reward. Quadruped locomotion is notoriously challenging because it requires managing intermittent contact switching and ground slip. These exact challenges make it an ideal benchmark for evaluating fast RL training and reliable sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: From days of training down to 10 minutes: JAX-native parallel simulation
sections.summary: The key to dramatically speeding up reinforcement learning lies in two factors: massively parallel simulation and GPU-native execution. Running everything from physical simulation to neural network updates entirely on the GPU completely removes CPU-GPU communication overhead.
sections.details:
To apply reinforcement learning to robotics safely and at a practical speed, this study brings together two technical breakthroughs.

### 1. Parallel Training Paradigm
Modern robotics simulators can run thousands of robot environments concurrently on a GPU. The RL algorithm receives observations from these parallel environments as a batched tensor and computes actions for each environment in a single pass. This massively parallel data collection shrinks exploration and data gathering from days or weeks down to just minutes of wall-clock time.

### 2. GPU-Native Reinforcement Learning Framework
This is where JAX, Python's machine learning library, plays a pivotal role. JAX code is optimized and compiled ahead of time for the GPU (via XLA), and primitives like `vmap` allow entire functions to run in parallel directly on the GPU. In conventional workflows, the physics simulator runs on the CPU, and data must be transferred to the GPU for neural network training and inference, creating a severe communication bottleneck. In the Playground framework adopted here, simulation, learning algorithms, and inference all reside within GPU memory. Eliminating all communication latency yields astounding throughput.

### Implications for Space Robotics
Simulation has long been extensively used in space systems for design and pre-validation. While simulating non-rigid (soft) bodies remains challenging, many contact dynamics—such as locomotion, navigation, manipulation, and docking—can already be simulated with sufficient fidelity. Fast parallel RL thus provides a realistic path toward rapidly developing behaviors for space robots operating in remote locations.

captions.F2: Comparison between a traditional RL workflow (left) and the JAX-based workflow used in this work (right). By compiling and executing both simulation and RL entirely on the GPU, the CPU-GPU bottleneck is completely eliminated.

sections.heading: PPO and domain randomization: A simple yet powerful sim-to-real recipe
sections.summary: The authors adopted PPO, an algorithm well suited for parallel environments and a de facto standard in robotics. To bridge the reality gap between simulation and real hardware, they combined it with domain randomization by perturbing parameters such as robot mass and surface friction across environments.
sections.details:
At the core of the methodology is Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). PPO is a policy gradient method that clips policy updates, preventing catastrophic learning collapse from overly large parameter steps and ensuring stable training. It was chosen because it is accessible, straightforward to use, and exceptionally efficient at handling massive batches from parallel environments.

When deploying a simulation-trained policy directly to hardware, policies often fail due to subtle physical discrepancies between simulation and reality (the reality gap). To overcome this, the authors introduced Domain Randomization (DR).

In domain randomization, physical parameters are deliberately varied across thousands of parallel simulation environments:
- Robot physical properties: link masses, component dimensions, center of mass position, etc.
- Terrain properties: ground friction coefficient, slope angles, etc.

By preventing the policy from overfitting to a single simulation environment and instead training it to succeed across a distribution of diverse physics settings, the agent naturally develops robustness against real-world modeling errors and environmental variations. Combining PPO with DR serves as a remarkably simple yet reliable and practical recipe for sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: Case study 1: Walking without slipping on low-friction sheets
sections.summary: In a flat-terrain locomotion task tracking joystick velocity commands, the authors evaluated the slip resistance of a policy trained with friction randomization. Tested on wet plastic sheets mimicking ice, the friction-DR policy completed all 10 trials stably without a single fall.
sections.details:
### Setup and Task Definition
The first experiment evaluated locomotion on flat terrain with varying friction. Traversing surfaces with unpredictable friction—such as sand, ice, or wet floors—is essential both for planetary exploration and on Earth. The robot learns to track 3D joystick velocity commands (forward/backward velocity, lateral velocity, and yaw angular velocity) on a flat plane.

- Observations (45-dim): base angular velocity, projected gravity vector, joint positions and velocities for all 12 joints, and target velocity commands from the joystick
- Actions (12-dim): target joint positions for all 12 joints (converted to target torques via a PD controller)
- Reward formulation: encourages tracking target velocities while penalizing foot slip, falls, and excessive motor torques

Training ran on a single RTX 4070 Ti across 8,192 parallel environments for a total of 250 million steps. The entire process took only about 11 minutes: around 3 minutes for code compilation and about 8 minutes for training.

### Comparative Experiment: BaseDR vs. FrictionDR
Two policies were trained: "BaseDR", which only randomized robot mass and center of mass, and "FrictionDR", which additionally randomized the foot-ground friction coefficient within $[0.6, 1.0]$. Both were tested on real hardware across high-friction carpet and low-friction wet plastic sheets mimicking ice.

### Experimental Results
During testing on the low-friction surface (10 trials each), the BaseDR policy slipped and fell violently 3 times while walking forward. In contrast, the FrictionDR policy successfully walked without falling in all 10 trials (showing only minor slip when walking backward). On high-friction carpet, both policies performed similarly, proving that adding friction randomization is what allowed the policy to stand its ground effectively on unseen slippery surfaces.

captions.F3: Robot base inclination angle (vertical axis, degrees) over time while walking on a slippery wet plastic sheet. Thin lines represent individual trials; thick lines show the median. BaseDR without friction randomization (orange) slips and falls (tilting to ~175 degrees) when moving forward, whereas FrictionDR (green) keeps tilt low and completes all runs with zero falls.

sections.heading: Case study 2: Crossing steep slopes in a lunar-analog facility
sections.summary: Using curriculum learning that gradually steepens simulated terrain slopes, the authors tested real-world transfer in the loose soil and slopes of a lunar-analog facility. While the policy without slope DR fell almost every time on the slope, the slope-aware policy avoided falls entirely, either crossing successfully or stopping safely.
sections.details:
### Environment and Curriculum Learning
The next challenge was traversing rugged, uneven terrain. To minimize simulation design effort, the authors kept the exact same rewards and observation space as the flat-terrain task, altering only the ground slope.

They introduced curriculum learning to expose the agent to progressively steeper inclinations:
- First 200M steps: 0 degrees (flat terrain)
- Next 50M steps: randomly chosen from 0, 5, and 10 degrees
- Next 50M steps: randomly chosen from 0, 5, 10, and 15 degrees
- Final 50M steps: randomly chosen from 0, 5, 10, 15, and 20 degrees

This automatic curriculum of 350 million total steps also finished in roughly 15 minutes on a single GPU. The resulting "SlopesDR" policy was compared against "FrictionDR" and a baseline "NoDR" policy trained solely on flat ground without any randomization.

### Hardware Validation in a Lunar-Analog Facility
Experiments took place in a lunar-analog facility featuring granular material mimicking lunar regolith and rocky undulating terrain. Two scenarios were tested: a flat-ground locomotion sequence and a difficult slope-traversal scenario requiring the robot to walk across a steep sandy slope.

### Experimental Results
On flat ground, all policies—including NoDR—walked without problems. However, outcomes diverged sharply during the slope-traversal scenario:
- NoDR: Having only seen flat ground, it immediately lost balance upon entering the slope, falling in 9 out of 10 trials.
- FrictionDR: While friction randomization helped it withstand some attempts, it still experienced sporadic falls.
- SlopesDR: Avoided falling in all 10 trials. The robot either traversed the slope completely or intentionally halted its gait to remain stably parked on the incline. This appears to be an emergent defensive adaptation learned during simulation to avoid fall penalties.

captions.F4: Experimental scenarios in the lunar-analog facility. Left: flat loose-soil test covering forward, lateral, and turning gaits. Right: slope-traversal test across an inclined sandy slope (heatmap shows slope angle, with bluer colors indicating steeper inclines).
captions.F5: Robot base inclination data in the lunar-analog facility. In the flat scenario (left), all policies remain stable. In the slope-traversal scenario (right), NoDR without randomization (red) falls severely shortly after starting (~175 degrees tilt), while SlopesDR (blue) minimizes tilt and avoids falling entirely.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook: Toward the future of space robotics
sections.summary: This work proved that reinforcement learning on a consumer GPU for under 20 minutes can yield zero-shot controllers capable of tackling unseen real-world rough terrains and lunar-analog environments. Future steps include stacking high-level behaviors like autonomous exploration onto these low-level locomotion policies and combining them with classical model predictive control.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated that modern RL techniques allow complex control policies to be learned quickly in simulation and transferred reliably to the real world zero-shot. Eliminating days-long training runs in favor of 10-to-15-minute trial-and-error iterations dramatically accelerates development cycles.

### Future Directions and Research Questions
Building on these findings, the paper highlights several promising directions:
- Higher-level task integration: Using the learned locomotion policy as a low-level controller while integrating higher-level tasks such as object search, autonomous navigation, construction, firefighting, or agriculture (supplementary video includes a proof-of-concept where the robot autonomously searches for and approaches a ball).
- Exploring other RL algorithms: Evaluating parallelizable algorithms such as Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) or introducing continual learning directly onboard the hardware.
- Expanding action spaces: Exploring alternatives to target joint positions, such as joint velocity commands or direct torque control.
- Hybridization with classical control: Quantitatively comparing RL controllers with model-based controllers like Model Predictive Control (MPC), establishing hybrid methods that combine the strengths of both.

These results offer a compelling glimpse into a future where reinforcement learning becomes an indispensable, practical tool in high-stakes space exploration.

takeaways: JAX-native physics simulation removes CPU-GPU communication overhead, allowing hundreds of millions of RL steps to finish in about 10 to 15 minutes on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4070 Ti).

Without complex reward engineering or high-fidelity environment modeling, proper domain randomization (varying friction and slope) and curriculum learning enable reliable zero-shot transfer even to harsh environments like a lunar-analog facility.

Shrinking simulation training iterations to minutes drastically speeds up trial-and-error in robot controller design, substantially lowering the barrier to entry for space and terrestrial robotics development.
limitations: The evaluated task is limited to low-level locomotion tracking joystick commands; it does not integrate autonomous navigation, such as vision-based obstacle avoidance or long-term path planning.

In the slope-traversal test, the policy exhibited conservative behavior in some trials—halting completely mid-slope to avoid fall penalties—highlighting an unresolved trade-off against forward-progress incentives in reward design.

Space-specific conditions, such as reduced gravity (1/6 G on the Moon or 3/8 G on Mars) and the mechanical impact of abrasive, ultra-fine regolith dust on joint actuators, were not fully evaluated in simulation or hardware.
